buried-uk-ecosystem-collapse-report.headline: Suppressed UK intelligence report warned ecosystem collapse threatens food security
buried-uk-ecosystem-collapse-report.body_md:
Somewhere in Whitehall, twice in the space of a year, someone decided that a warning from Britain's own intelligence machinery was too alarming to publish. The document in question was not about a hostile state or a terror cell. It was about hedgerows, coral reefs and the Amazon — and what happens to food prices and social order when the natural systems that grow, water and stabilise the world's crops start to fail.

That document, *Global Biodiversity Loss, Ecosystem Collapse and National Security*, was compiled with input from the Joint Intelligence Committee, the body that sits above MI5, MI6 and GCHQ and produces the assessments a prime minister reads before deciding what actually threatens the country. According to reporting by the Guardian's Fiona Harvey, aides to then-prime minister Keir Starmer quashed plans to release it twice — first ahead of a planned October 2025 launch, then again afterwards — reportedly for fear that Reform UK would attack the government for prioritising climate concerns over the cost of living. It only became public in January 2026, in a redacted 14-page form, after a sustained freedom of information campaign by Ruth Chambers of the Green Alliance think tank forced Defra's hand.

> "A devastating picture of severe food shortages, price rises, migration, political destabilisation and possible war."

That is how Harvey characterised the substance of the assessment. It is a striking sentence to find applied to a government document about ecosystems rather than armies — and it is why the episode matters well beyond the usual audience for biodiversity policy.

## What the intelligence service actually said

The redacted version, published via gov.uk on 20-21 January, rates the risk to UK national security from global ecosystem degradation as "high" under a reasonable worst-case scenario, using the same probability-and-confidence framework the JIC applies to state threats. It names six systems — the Amazon and Congo rainforests, boreal forests, the Himalayas, and Southeast Asia's coral reefs and mangroves — as being on pathways toward collapse, meaning irreversible loss of function rather than gradual decline.

![NASA satellite imagery shows deforestation fronts cut into the Amazon rainforest in Rondônia, Brazil.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/ce/Amazon_deforestation_2010214.jpg)

The mechanism the assessment worries about is not exotic. The UK imports around 40% of its food, more than a quarter of it from Europe. Officials reportedly judged it a "realistic possibility" that by 2030 the natural systems underpinning that supply — soil, pollinators, stable rainfall, functioning fisheries — could already be degrading enough to disrupt it, with some ecosystems capable of tipping within five years. The knock-on effects described include higher global food prices, intensified competition for scarce resources, migration, a rise in organised crime around resource smuggling, and — because degraded ecosystems bring humans, livestock and wildlife into closer contact — greater pandemic risk.

Defra's public defence has been that Britain's food system is resilient by design. "We have access through international trade to food products that cannot be produced here," a spokesperson said, arguing that diversified sourcing insulates the UK from any single shock. The National Farmers' Union was less sanguine. Its deputy president, David Exwood, put it bluntly: "With an increasingly volatile geopolitical and climatic situation, we cannot rely on imports to sustain us."

## A pattern of shelving, not a one-off

What turns this from a policy dispute into a governance story is the repetition. Caroline Lucas, the former Green Party leader who has tracked the episode closely, argued that the biodiversity assessment was not suppressed in isolation — that a second, related report on UK food security was also held back around the same period. "To cover up one high-level report looks odd," she said. "To cover up two looks like a pattern."

The pattern, as reported, was political rather than analytical: nobody inside government appears to have disputed the JIC's judgment. The objection was to public alarm at a moment when the cost of living, not the Amazon canopy, was the dominant political story. That is a defensible short-term political calculation and a poor way to manage a long-tail systemic risk — the two things are not the same, and conflating them is the failure worth naming.

![Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrives at 10 Downing Street.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_arrives_at_10_Downing_Street_%2855406667976%29.jpg)

Starmer resigned as Labour leader and prime minister in June, and Andy Burnham took office on 20 July. The decisions to shelve the report were his predecessor's, but the question of whether to publish the assessment in full — Parliament has already pressed the government on this in both the Commons and the Lords this year — now sits with him. So far, Defra has not committed to releasing an unredacted version.

## What it means for anyone pricing risk

For traders, the interesting part is not the ecology. It is what the episode reveals about how systemic, low-probability-high-severity risks get treated inside the institutions meant to monitor them. A government that will not surface its own intelligence assessment of a food-security threat to its own parliament is not a government whose risk models can be assumed to be feeding into anything markets watch — sovereign debt pricing, agricultural futures, or supply-chain contingency planning. Commodity markets already have plenty on their plate this month, from oil sliding on hopes of an Iran-Hormuz deal to gilt yields at their highest since 1998 ahead of the Autumn Budget. Ecosystem collapse does not trade on any of those screens, and this episode is a reminder that the absence of a price signal is not the same as the absence of a risk.

The UK's own third 35°C-plus heatwave of the year, with rail speed restrictions already in force, is the visible, immediate face of the stress the JIC assessment describes in the abstract. The intelligence document is about the slower, structural version of the same problem — and it took a freedom of information campaign, not a government press release, to get even a redacted account of it into public view.

The next marker to watch is whether Burnham's government responds to the parliamentary pressure by publishing a fuller version of the assessment, or whether the report that took an FOI fight to surface once quietly settles back into the file. Green Alliance and opposition MPs have said they will keep pushing; the Autumn Budget, due in the coming months, will be the first real test of whether food-security risk features in fiscal planning at all.

mi6-top-intelligence-survey.headline: MI6 ranked Europe's top foreign intelligence service in peer survey
mi6-top-intelligence-survey.body_md:
There is no leaderboard for spies, no annual results call, no earnings guidance. So when 60 serving and former intelligence officers from 25 countries were asked, in effect, to hand out a Ballon d'Or for espionage, the result was always going to travel. The French magazine L'Express spent three months coaxing around 100 practitioners — CIA and Mossad officers among them — into ranking their European counterparts. The consensus: Britain's MI6 sits well clear of the field, prized above all for recruiting sources deep inside Russia, China, Iran and Turkey.

> "The United Kingdom has by far the strongest intelligence services in Europe. MI6 is exceptional." — Robert Grenier, former CIA station chief

It is an odd thing to put a number on, and the number itself — MI6 on 251 points, France's DGSE on 169 — matters less than what the exercise says about how Europe's spy services see their own hierarchy after four years of war on the continent and a widening contest with Beijing.

## How you score a secret

L'Express borrowed the format of a Eurovision or a Ballon d'Or: each of the 60 voting professionals, including 17 serving or former agency chiefs, submitted a top five. Points were tallied, and a ranking fell out the other end. MI6 topped it, followed by the DGSE, the Dutch AIVD and MIVD, Ukraine's services in fourth, and Germany's BND in fifth. Sweden, Norway, Estonia, Poland and Denmark rounded out the top ten, each drawing praise for a specific niche — Estonia for cyber and open-source work, Norway for Arctic and maritime coverage, Sweden for its rising weight in the Baltic.

Greece scored no points at all, tied with Ireland and Luxembourg at the bottom of the table. And yet the report singles Athens out for something the numbers don't capture: a standing invitation to the table whenever the subject is Turkey. Geography and decades of friction across the Aegean have given Greek services a granularity on Ankara's politics, military posture and intelligence services that larger, better-funded agencies can't easily replicate. It is the survey's most interesting footnote — proof that in this business, proximity can outrank budget.

![Historical peninsula and modern skyline of Istanbul, seen from the Bosphorus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Historical_peninsula_and_modern_skyline_of_Istanbul.jpg)

## The long game

What separates MI6 from the pack, according to the practitioners L'Express spoke to, is patience with people rather than any particular piece of tradecraft. Sources cited the agency's willingness to cultivate an informant for a decade or more before that relationship pays off — described by one voter as playing it "rather like the Russians do." Two cases surfaced repeatedly in the reporting: Alireza Akbari, the former Iranian deputy defence minister executed by Tehran in 2023 after being convicted of spying for MI6, and a Chinese civil-service couple recruited over years inside Beijing's bureaucracy. Neither case was volunteered by London — both surfaced through the states that caught the leak, which is itself a comment on how rarely this kind of penetration becomes visible at all.

> "The British are out in front on the Ukrainian issue." — Ralph Goff, former head of CIA operations in Europe

The DGSE's runner-up finish came with its own compliment, less about longevity than reach. A 34-year CIA veteran, Gina Bennett, told L'Express the French service was "the most capable partner" she'd encountered in human intelligence — a reputation built on France's post-colonial networks across the Sahel, the Gulf and North Africa, terrain where London has comparatively thinner cover.

![Sir Richard Moore, Chief of the Secret Intelligence Service 2020–2025](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/26/Richard_Moore_Portrait.jpg)

The institutional memory behind the ranking belongs partly to Sir Richard Moore, who ran MI6 from 2020 until stepping down last year — notably, a former UK ambassador to Turkey himself — and partly to his successor, Blaise Metreweli, the service's first female chief, who took over in October 2025 having previously run its technology directorate. The reputation the survey measures was built well before either of them arrived; what it doesn't measure is whether it survives the transition.

## What the score doesn't show

The caveats are worth sitting with. L'Express has not published a scoring rubric, a full list of who voted, or how ties and abstentions were handled — this is a magazine's reported survey of professional opinion, not an audited index. Critics elsewhere have made the more pointed version of that objection: the ranking measures reputation, not output, and reputation tracks budget. Britain's intelligence spending runs into the billions; the Baltic services praised for punching above their weight operate on tens of millions. A service can be well regarded by its peers and still miss the thing that matters most, or be feared by its targets while barely registering in a poll of allies.

None of that makes the exercise irrelevant to anyone pricing risk in Moscow, Tehran or the Bosphorus. Perception among the people who actually trade intelligence with each other is itself a input into how fast a warning travels between capitals, and how much a partner service is willing to share before a crisis breaks rather than after. A Europe where human coverage of Russia and Iran is concentrated in one or two capitals is a Europe slower, on average, to see trouble coming everywhere else — a gap post-Brexit debates about UK-EU security cooperation have circled for years without resolving.

The next test of that gap is already on the calendar. Sanctions diplomacy around Iran's nuclear file and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and the daily calculus of what Moscow will risk next in Ukraine, are precisely the theatres where the sources MI6 is credited with recruiting would earn their keep — or be shown, uncomfortably, not to have existed at all.
